failures.title: Renault K9K 1.5 dCi Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Diesel Particulate Filter (DPF) Clogging - the urban driving penalty
items.whatHappens: The K9K's DPF relies on sustained high temperatures to perform active regeneration - a process that requires a continuous 10-15 mile drive at consistent speed. For owners who primarily undertake short urban journeys, the engine may never reach the necessary temperatures, causing the DPF to become progressively clogged with soot and ash. Symptoms include the engine management light illuminating, hesitation or spluttering above 35mph, and a notable loss of power.
items.repairVsReplace: DPF cleaning by a specialist costs £200-£500. In severe cases, replacement is required (£600-£1,200). Preventative: a regular 20‑minute, 40mph run every week significantly helps maintain DPF health. → Read our full /failures/dpf-failure guide

items.title: Oil Pressure Relief Valve Failure - catastrophic engine failure risk
items.whatHappens: A more serious, though less common, issue is the failure of the oil pressure relief valve, which is integrated with the oil pump. If the valve seizes, oil pressure drops catastrophically, leading to sudden loss of drive, inability to accelerate, and the engine shutting down or stalling. In some cases, the oil filter housing can be deformed by overpressure. This can write off the engine if not caught immediately.
items.repairVsReplace: Oil pump replacement is a significant job (£500-£1,200). If the engine has suffered oil starvation, a full replacement unit is the only safe option - bearing damage is almost certain.

items.title: Injector Failure - Delphi units are particularly vulnerable
items.whatHappens: The K9K's common‑rail injection system uses either Bosch or Delphi injectors. Delphi units are particularly sensitive to fuel quality - low‑grade diesel can cause injector failure within 10,000 km. Symptoms include rough idle, misfires, loss of power, and engine management lights. In severe cases, a failed injector can allow exhaust gases back into the fuel rail, causing the engine not to start. A worn injector can also release fine metal particles into the fuel system, damaging the high‑pressure pump and other injectors.
items.repairVsReplace: Injector replacement costs £150-£400 per injector plus coding. The entire common‑rail system may need flushing if contamination has occurred.

items.title: EGR Valve and Cooler Blockage
items.whatHappens: The EGR (exhaust gas recirculation) valve and cooler can become clogged with carbon deposits, particularly on vehicles used primarily for short journeys. Symptoms include rough idle, hesitation on acceleration, and reduced fuel economy.
items.repairVsReplace: EGR valve cleaning (£150-£300) or replacement (£250-£500). The EGR cooler replacement is more labour‑intensive (£400-£800).

items.title: Timing Belt - critical interval
items.whatHappens: The K9K uses a timing belt, not a chain. A broken timing belt will cause pistons to strike valves - catastrophic engine damage. The belt replacement interval is 72,000 miles or 6 years, though many specialists recommend 60,000 miles or 5 years, particularly for vehicles used on short journeys.
items.repairVsReplace: Timing belt replacement is routine maintenance (£300-£600). If the belt has broken, the engine is almost certainly written off - valve and piston damage is nearly universal.

failures.goodYearsLine: The K9K has been in production since 2001, with continuous improvements. The 2018+ Euro 6d‑TEMP and Euro 6d variants feature improved injectors, revised turbochargers and updated engine management. The "Blue dCi" variants (from approximately 2019) addressed some oil consumption concerns. However, the fundamental DPF and injector issues persist across all generations. Early K9K engines (2001-2005) suffered from conrod bearing failure - this is much less common on 2018+ units. The K9K remains one of Europe's most popular and well‑understood diesel engines, with extensive parts availability and specialist knowledge nationwide.

variants.title: K9K Sub‑Codes Explained - Which One Is in Your Car?
variants.intro: INTRO: The K9K family covers dozens of sub‑codes, each representing different power outputs, emissions standards, and hardware revisions. The 2018+ updated variants - fitted to the Nissan Juke, Qashqai and Renault models mentioned above - carry codes such as K9K 410, K9K 636, K9K 646, K9K 647, K9K 648, K9K 649, K9K 656, K9K 657, K9K 658, K9K 666, K9K 667 and K9K 896. Understanding your exact sub‑code is essential when sourcing a replacement - different variants have different ECU calibrations and, in some cases, different hardware. - Fitted to: Nissan Qashqai J11, Nissan Juke F15, Renault Kadjar, Renault Mégane IV - Key technical difference: 110 hp (81 kW) @ 4,000 rpm, 240-260 Nm torque. Euro 6 compliant with DPF and SCR (AdBlue) on some applications. Features Bosch common‑rail injection. - Sub‑code‑specific failure note: Shares the family failure pattern above - DPF clogging is the most common complaint on these urban‑friendly SUVs. Injector failure (Delphi on some variants) is also reported. - Interchange note: K9K 636 and K9K 646 are not directly interchangeable - the ECU calibration, injector coding and emissions hardware differ. Always verify the exact sub‑code before purchasing a replacement. - Fitted to: Renault Kadjar, Renault Scénic IV - Key technical difference: 115 hp (85 kW), 270 Nm torque. The highest‑output Euro 6 K9K variant. Features variable‑geometry turbocharger and revised ECU calibration. - Sub‑code‑specific failure note: Shares the family failure pattern. The higher state of tune may accelerate turbocharger wear on higher‑mileage examples. - Interchange note: Not a direct swap with lower‑output K9K variants - the turbocharger, injectors and ECU are specific to this tune. - Fitted to: Dacia Duster II, Renault Mégane IV - Key technical difference: 110 hp (81 kW), 240 Nm torque. Euro 6b compliant. These codes are typically found in Dacia and entry‑level Renault applications. - Sub‑code‑specific failure note: Shares family pattern. DPF issues are common on Duster models used for urban driving. - Interchange note: K9K 656 and K9K 658 are mechanically similar but have different ECU calibrations - verify compatibility before fitting. - Fitted to: Renault Clio IV, Renault Captur I - Key technical difference: 109 hp (80 kW), 240 Nm torque. Compact application with specific ECU calibration for smaller vehicles. - Sub‑code‑specific failure note: Shares family pattern. The compact engine bay in Clio and Captur can make DPF access more difficult. - Interchange note: Not a direct swap with Qashqai‑spec K9K variants - the ECU calibration and some ancillaries differ. - Fitted to: Dacia Duster I / II - Key technical difference: 110 hp, 240 Nm torque. Specifically calibrated for Duster applications with different gearing and emissions hardware. - Sub‑code‑specific failure note: Shares family pattern. DPF and EGR issues are the most common complaints. - Interchange note: These codes are often interchangeable with K9K 656/658 but always verify ECU compatibility.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement K9K 1.5 dCi - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: A used K9K can be a cost‑effective option for lower‑value host vehicles (sub‑£3,000 Clio, Megane, Qashqai) - but only if the engine comes with documented proof of timing belt replacement, injector health, and DPF maintenance. Without this documentation, a used engine is a gamble - DPF and injector issues are not "if" but "when". Used prices from £680-£1,200 reflect this risk. Link once:

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: A properly reconditioned K9K is the recommended choice for most owners. A full recon should address the engine's known weak points: new timing belt and tensioners, new injectors (with coding), new oil pump and pressure relief valve, DPF cleaning or replacement, EGR valve cleaning, and full gasket set. Given the £1,500-£3,500 supply cost and the host vehicle value (£2,000-£12,000 for a decent example), this represents a significant but justifiable investment for a well‑maintained vehicle. A 12-24 month warranty is essential. Link once:

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full K9K rebuild is justified for low‑mileage, well‑maintained examples or where the owner plans long‑term ownership. An upgraded rebuild should include new pistons, rings, bearings, timing belt, oil pump, and a full valvetrain refresh. Rebuild costs (£2,500-£4,500+) are significant - only consider this for high‑value or sentimental vehicles. Link once:

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: All supply options can be fitted through our network of vetted Renault‑Nissan diesel specialists nationwide, with a minimum 12‑month warranty on reconditioned and rebuilt units and full nationwide delivery coverage. Link once:
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: The K9K sits in host vehicles ranging from £1,500-£5,000 (older Clio, Megane, Sandero) to £6,000-£15,000 (Qashqai, Kadjar, Captur, Juke)【THIRD‑PARTY - AutoTrader UK market data 2025】. A £1,500-£3,500 reconditioned unit represents 20-70%+ of the vehicle's value on many examples - on a £2,000 Clio, a £2,000 replacement is 100% of the vehicle's value, making it a borderline or non‑viable decision. The honest marketplace‑neutrality position is: if your K9K has suffered catastrophic failure (timing belt break, oil pump seizure) and your vehicle is worth under £3,000, evaluate scrap or part‑exchange value before committing to a replacement. For well‑maintained Qashqai, Kadjar or Captur examples with good bodywork and service history, the replacement can be a worthwhile investment.

items.question: How do I know which K9K sub‑code I have (K9K 636, 646, 647, 649, 656, 657, 658, 666, 667, 896, 898, etc.)?
items.answer: The engine code is stamped on a machined pad on the engine block (typically on the front or side, visible from the top of the engine bay) and appears on the V5C under "Engine number" - the code will read K9K followed by a three‑digit number (e.g. K9K636xxxxxx). Use a Renault/Nissan VIN decoder to confirm the exact variant from the build sheet. → Verify your K9K sub‑code now.

K9K 666/667 = 109 hp, Clio and Captur applications.
K9K 896/898 = 110 hp, Duster and later Dacia variants.

items.question: Is the K9K 1.5 dCi reliable, and what mileage can I expect?
items.answer: The K9K is one of Europe's most proven diesel engines. With diligent maintenance - 10,000‑mile oil changes using Renault RN17 approved oil, timely timing belt replacement (72,000 miles or 6 years), and regular DPF‑friendly driving - many engines reach 150,000-200,000+ miles. The engine is well‑understood with extensive parts availability and specialist knowledge nationwide. → Find a specialist who knows the K9K inside out.

DPF cleaning should be considered every 60,000-80,000 miles for urban vehicles.
Regular 20‑minute, 40mph motorway runs help maintain DPF health.

mainEntity.name: How much does a Renault K9K 1.5 dCi engine replacement cost in the UK?

acceptedAnswer.text: A reconditioned K9K supply‑only typically costs between £1,500 and £3,500, with fitted prices ranging from £1,900 to £4,000 depending on labour and additional parts. Used units start from £680 supply‑only, while full rebuilds run £2,500-£4,500. Used pricing is [THIRD‑PARTY] from Motorinsul UK; reconditioned pricing is estimated. Prices vary significantly by sub‑code - 115 hp variants (K9K 647/649) may command a premium. Supply‑only excludes fitting; add 7-10 hours at £65-£85/hr for specialist installation. Always compare quotes - prices can vary by 20% between specialists.

mainEntity.name: What is the most common failure on the Renault K9K 1.5 dCi?

acceptedAnswer.text: DPF clogging is the most common issue on the K9K, particularly on vehicles used primarily for short urban journeys - the engine may never reach the necessary temperatures for active regeneration. Injector failure (especially on Delphi units) and oil pressure relief valve seizure (leading to catastrophic engine failure) are also well‑documented issues. EGR valve and cooler blockage is common on higher‑mileage examples. DPF cleaning costs £200-£500; replacement costs £600-£1,200. Injector replacement costs £150-£400 per injector plus coding. Timing belt replacement is critical - interval is 72,000 miles or 6 years.

mainEntity.name: Which models use the Renault K9K 1.5 dCi engine?

acceptedAnswer.text: The K9K is the most widely used diesel engine in Europe. It is fitted across Renault (Clio, Captur, Mégane, Kadjar, Scénic, Kangoo), Nissan (Qashqai, Juke, Micra, Note), Dacia (Duster, Sandero, Logan, Dokker), Mercedes‑Benz (Citan/OM607) and Suzuki (Swift, SX4, Vitara with K9K‑derived units). The 2018+ updated variants are Euro 6d‑TEMP / Euro 6d compliant. Check your V5C or engine block stamp to confirm your exact sub‑code. Mercedes‑badged OM607 is the same engine with different ECU calibration. The engine has been in production since 2001, with continuous improvements.

mainEntity.name: Should I buy a used, reconditioned, or rebuilt K9K?

acceptedAnswer.text: For most K9K owners, a reconditioned unit with new timing belt, injectors, oil pump and DPF is the recommended choice - it addresses the engine's key weaknesses and comes with a 12-24 month warranty. Used units (£680-£1,200) are cheaper but carry high risk without documented timing belt and injector history. Rebuilds (£2,500-£4,500+) are only justified for low‑mileage, high‑value examples or sentimental vehicles. Used: only with documented timing belt replacement and injector history. Reconditioned: best balance - all common weak points addressed, warranty included. Rebuilt: ideal for low‑mileage, well‑maintained examples or long‑term keepers.

mainEntity.name: How do I know which K9K sub‑code I have (K9K 636, 646, 647, 649, 656, 657, 658, 666, 667, 896, 898, etc.)?

acceptedAnswer.text: The engine code is stamped on a machined pad on the engine block (typically on the front or side, visible from the top of the engine bay) and appears on the V5C under 'Engine number' - the code will read K9K followed by a three‑digit number (e.g. K9K636xxxxxx). Use a Renault/Nissan VIN decoder to confirm the exact variant from the build sheet. K9K 636/646/648 = 110 hp, fitted to Qashqai, Juke, Kadjar, Mégane. K9K 647/649 = 115 hp, high‑output variant with VGT turbo. K9K 656/657/658 = 110 hp, Dacia and entry‑level Renault applications. K9K 666/667 = 109 hp, Clio and Captur applications. K9K 896/898 = 110 hp, Duster and later Dacia variants.

mainEntity.name: Is the K9K 1.5 dCi reliable, and what mileage can I expect?

acceptedAnswer.text: The K9K is one of Europe's most proven diesel engines. With diligent maintenance - 10,000‑mile oil changes using Renault RN17 approved oil, timely timing belt replacement (72,000 miles or 6 years), and regular DPF‑friendly driving - many engines reach 150,000-200,000+ miles. The engine is well‑understood with extensive parts availability and specialist knowledge nationwide. Budget for timing belt replacement at 72,000 miles or 6 years - £300-£600. DPF cleaning should be considered every 60,000-80,000 miles for urban vehicles. Regular 20‑minute, 40mph motorway runs help maintain DPF health. The K9K is significantly more reliable than the earlier F9Q 1.9 dCi.
